questions.explanationCorrect: Secrets and regulated data must not go into prompts without authorization; redact them or route through approved, compliant channels.
questions.explanationDistractor: Base64 is not encryption; encoding a secret still transmits it and does nothing to satisfy data-handling policy.

questions.stem: A nightly job fires thousands of requests in a burst and trips rate limits, failing many. Besides backoff, what design change most directly prevents tripping the limit?

options.A: Remove the error handling from the job so that the many request failures at least stay silent
options.B: Smooth the load with client-side concurrency limits or queueing, or move the bulk work to the Batches API
options.C: Send every request at once as before, but bump up the max_tokens on each of the calls
options.D: Duplicate each outgoing request so that at least one of the two copies manages to succeed

questions.explanationCorrect: Rate limits are about request pacing, so limiting concurrency or moving latency-tolerant bulk work to the Batches API prevents the burst from tripping them.
questions.explanationDistractor: Duplicating requests increases the request volume, making rate-limit pressure worse rather than better.

questions.stem: You are building an eval to gate prompt changes for an extraction feature. Which eval design is soundest?

options.A: A single hand-picked example that is known to always pass whenever you run the eval
options.B: Only adversarial edge cases and nothing else, deliberately leaving out every everyday input that real users send
options.C: A representative set of labeled inputs with clear, automatable pass/fail criteria covering common and important edge cases
options.D: Ask the model 'did you do well?' after each run and simply record whatever it answers

questions.explanationCorrect: A good eval uses representative labeled inputs with objective, automatable pass/fail criteria across common and important edge cases, so it reliably detects regressions.
questions.explanationDistractor: A single always-passing example cannot distinguish a good change from a bad one, so it provides no gate at all.

questions.stem: A chat feature feels sluggish because users watch a spinner while a long answer generates, and costs are high because every turn uses Opus. Which combination best addresses both?

options.A: Raise both max_tokens and the effort level so that each answer finishes generating sooner
options.B: Disable retries entirely so that you can save a bit of time on each individual model call
options.C: Cache the final answers just once and then replay those exact same answers back to all users
options.D: Stream responses to cut perceived latency and route simpler turns to a cheaper model

questions.explanationCorrect: Streaming reduces perceived latency by showing tokens as they arrive, and routing simpler turns to a cheaper model reduces cost, addressing both problems.
questions.explanationDistractor: Raising max_tokens and effort tends to make responses longer and slower, worsening the perceived latency it is meant to fix.

questions.stem: For a large offline re-processing job, a teammate proposes relying solely on prompt caching to cut costs. Why is that incomplete?

options.A: For big latency-tolerant bulk jobs the Batches API is the larger cost lever (~50% off) and provides async processing that caching does not
options.B: Prompt caching actually increases the total cost for a large bulk job rather than reducing it
options.C: Caching and batching cannot be reasoned about separately from one another, so neither one can ever truly substitute for the other
options.D: Prompt caching only works on the Haiku model tier, so it is entirely irrelevant to this job

questions.explanationCorrect: For big, latency-tolerant jobs the Batches API is the primary lever (~50% cheaper and asynchronous); prompt caching is a separate, smaller optimization.
questions.explanationDistractor: Prompt caching lowers cost on repeated prefixes rather than raising it, so the claim that it increases cost is simply wrong.

questions.stem: Your agent can trigger refunds, and you want to catch unsafe or incorrect model outputs before they reach the payment system. Which control is this?

options.A: Input screening applied to the incoming user message before the model ever runs
options.B: Output screening: validate or filter the model's output before it acts on downstream systems
options.C: Prompt caching, applied here specifically to speed up the refund path so the decisions come back faster
options.D: Streaming the refund decision back to the user token by token as it is generated

questions.explanationCorrect: Output screening validates or filters the model's proposed action before it reaches a downstream system like payments, catching unsafe or wrong outputs.
questions.explanationDistractor: Input screening inspects the incoming request, not the model's generated refund action, so it does not catch a bad output.

questions.stem: Your cached prefix includes a tools array and a JSON blob, and the hit rate is erratic between otherwise-identical requests. What subtle issue commonly causes this?

options.A: The tools array is never actually part of the cached prefix at all, so its specific contents simply cannot influence whether or not a cache hit happens on any given request you send
options.B: JSON is always canonicalized for you automatically before caching, so the ordering of keys or fields cannot possibly matter to the cache
options.C: Nondeterministic ordering, tools listed in a different order or unsorted JSON keys, changes the prefix bytes and breaks the cache; serialize them deterministically
options.D: The cache ignores both the tools array and any JSON blobs entirely, so erratic hit rates from this cause are simply not possible

questions.explanationCorrect: Caching is byte-sensitive: reordering the tools array or emitting unsorted JSON keys changes the prefix and prevents a hit, so serialize deterministically.
questions.explanationDistractor: JSON is not auto-canonicalized for you; key order in your serialized prefix matters to the cache match.

questions.stem: For irreversible, high-impact tool calls such as issuing payouts, how should the safety layer behave when a check is uncertain or temporarily unavailable?

options.A: Fail open and allow the payout to proceed, so that users are never blocked by the check
options.B: Skip the authorization step for speed and then audit each payout sometime after the fact
options.C: Let the model self-authorize the payout based on its own confidence in the decision
options.D: Gate the call behind explicit authorization and fail closed, denying on uncertainty

questions.explanationCorrect: High-impact, irreversible actions must be gated by explicit authorization and fail closed, denying when a check is uncertain, so a single failure cannot open the system.
questions.explanationDistractor: Failing open on uncertainty is exactly wrong for irreversible actions; it lets bad calls through when controls are weakest.

questions.stem: You keep pasting the same multi-step release-notes procedure into Claude Code each sprint and want the whole team to run it consistently going forward. How should you package it?

options.A: Author it as a Skill in .claude/skills/ committed to the repo, so it is versioned and available to everyone on pull
options.B: Save the whole multi-step release procedure as a plain text snippet inside your own personal notes application for later reuse
options.C: Put it in your own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so that it is always loaded for you on every task
options.D: Email the procedure out to all of your teammates at the very start of each new sprint

questions.explanationCorrect: Packaging a repeated workflow as a project Skill makes it version-controlled, discoverable, and reusable by the whole team on clone or pull, the core accelerator move.
questions.explanationDistractor: A personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md only helps you and loads for every task; it neither shares the workflow nor scopes it to releases.

questions.stem: You built a productivity win using an internal MCP server and want the team to adopt it without each person hand-configuring it or leaking tokens. What do you contribute to the repo?

options.A: A screenshot of your own local MCP settings for the others on the team to copy by hand
options.B: A committed .mcp.json defining the server, with secrets referenced as ${ENV} variables each developer supplies
options.C: Your personal access token pasted directly into the repository README for everyone to use
options.D: A short note telling everyone on the team to just go and add the internal MCP server to their own local config manually

questions.explanationCorrect: A committed .mcp.json with ${ENV} expansion shares the server config with the whole team while each developer supplies their own secret, so nothing sensitive is checked in.
questions.explanationDistractor: Pasting a personal token into the README leaks a secret into version control, the exact outcome ${ENV} expansion avoids.

questions.stem: Your shared skill evolved and a breaking behavior change disrupted a downstream team mid-sprint. What practice would have prevented the surprise?

options.A: Never change the shared skill again at all once it has been published to the team
options.B: Keep every one of the changes confined to each developer's own personal copy of the shared skill instead
options.C: Version the skill and communicate changes so consumers can adopt updates deliberately and pin a known-good version
options.D: Rename the skill on every single change so that all the old references break loudly

questions.explanationCorrect: Versioning shared accelerators lets consumers pin a known-good version and adopt updates intentionally, preventing breaking changes from landing unannounced.
questions.explanationDistractor: Freezing the skill forever is not maintainable; the goal is managed evolution through versioning, not stagnation.

questions.stem: You used Claude to generate a tricky migration and want a review most likely to catch its own blind spots before you ship. What is most effective?

options.A: Ask the same session that originally wrote the migration to re-read its own work and then grade that same output
options.B: Raise the effort level on the original session and simply regenerate the whole migration
options.C: Add the phrase 'double-check your work carefully' to the end of the original prompt
options.D: Have a second, independent Claude instance with no access to the first's reasoning review it, to avoid confirmation bias

questions.explanationCorrect: A second, independent instance without the generator's reasoning reviews with fresh eyes, catching blind spots that self-review tends to miss due to confirmation bias.
questions.explanationDistractor: Asking the same session to grade itself inherits the same assumptions and blind spots that produced the code, so it is weaker at finding them.

questions.stem: Your prototype works on your laptop, but leadership will not approve it until it is maintainable and could be operated without you. Which package best makes it defensible?

options.A: Evals as acceptance gates, documentation and runbooks, and shared config (CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json, skills) checked into the repo
options.B: A noticeably longer and more detailed system prompt paired together with a nicely polished demo video of the working prototype in action
options.C: Your own personal shell aliases together with the local notes you kept while building it
options.D: A standing promise that you will personally remain on call for the project indefinitely

questions.explanationCorrect: Evals as gates, documented runbooks, and shared version-controlled config let others operate and extend the system, which is what makes a prototype defensible.
questions.explanationDistractor: A demo video and a longer prompt do not make the system operable by others or guard against regressions the way evals and shared config do.

questions.stem: You want teammates to install a bundle of your team's skills and commands in one step, discoverable from a catalog. Which Claude Code mechanism supports this?

options.A: Emailing a zip archive of your .claude/skills/ folder around for teammates to unpack
options.B: A plugin published to a marketplace (a catalog defined by a marketplace.json) that teammates install
options.C: A gist with the files linked in the team chat for everyone to copy down individually
options.D: Copying the files into each teammate's home directory, one by one, over an SSH connection

questions.explanationCorrect: A plugin published to a marketplace bundles skills and commands so teammates can install them in one discoverable, repeatable step.
questions.explanationDistractor: Emailing a zip is manual and unversioned, offering none of the discovery or repeatable install that a marketplace plugin provides.

questions.stem: A prototype hard-codes long, evolving prompt instructions inside application source, so every tweak needs a code deploy. How do you make it more maintainable?

options.A: Duplicate the long prompt across every single service in the system so that each one separately owns and maintains its very own private copy of it
options.B: Inline even more of the surrounding logic so that all of it lives together in one file
options.C: Extract the durable guidance into versioned config (CLAUDE.md or a Skill) so it can evolve without a code deploy and is shared consistently
options.D: Store the prompt in a database table that no one on the team ever actually reviews

questions.explanationCorrect: Moving durable prompt guidance into versioned config like CLAUDE.md or a Skill lets it evolve without a code deploy and keeps it consistent and reviewable across the team.
questions.explanationDistractor: Duplicating the prompt across services multiplies the maintenance burden and invites the copies to drift out of sync.

questions.stem: You have a set of exemplar code patterns that should guide Claude only when writing a certain kind of integration, without bloating every session. What is the best home for them?

options.A: The system prompt of every single request, so the exemplars are always in front of the model
options.B: A .claude/rules/ glob that matches all files, so the patterns apply on every edit you make
options.C: A message pinned in the team chat channel that developers refer back to when they need it
options.D: A Skill that packages the exemplars and loads on demand when the relevant task is detected

questions.explanationCorrect: A Skill packages reusable exemplar context and loads only when its task is detected, so the patterns guide the right work without weighing down every session.
questions.explanationDistractor: Putting exemplars in the system prompt of every request loads them universally, wasting context on unrelated tasks.

questions.stem: You are rotating off a project. Which deliverable most ensures the team can operate and extend your Claude-based system after you leave?

options.A: A handoff of docs, runbooks, and shared version-controlled config (CLAUDE.md, skills, .mcp.json) the team can adopt
options.B: Your own personal chat history with the assistant, exported to a single file and then handed over to the team
options.C: A single verbal walkthrough of the whole system delivered to the team on your last day
options.D: Keeping the critical prompts only in your head as institutional knowledge for later

questions.explanationCorrect: Docs, runbooks, and shared version-controlled config make the system operable and extensible by others, so it survives your departure.
questions.explanationDistractor: A verbal walkthrough is not durable; once you leave, the team has nothing written to operate or extend the system.

questions.stem: You contribute a skill to the team repo but colleagues report Claude rarely uses it. Assuming the body is solid, what most improves adoption?

options.A: Make the skill file considerably longer overall so that there is simply a lot more content inside it for the model to match against
options.B: Write a precise description with the trigger keywords that match when it should fire, so it is discovered for the right tasks
options.C: Restrict the skill's allowed-tools list even further so it stays tightly focused on its job
options.D: Move the skill out of the shared repo and into your own personal skills directory instead

questions.explanationCorrect: A skill is surfaced by its description and trigger keywords, so a precise, keyword-rich description is what gets it invoked for the right tasks.
questions.explanationDistractor: Restricting allowed-tools narrows what the skill can do once running; it does nothing to help the skill get discovered.

questions.stem: Different teammates get inconsistent code style from Claude Code in the same repo. Which single change most cheaply enforces one standard for everyone?

options.A: Ask each developer to remember the standard and apply it consistently on their own
options.B: Add a PreToolUse hook that rejects any code it happens to dislike as it passes
options.C: Codify the standard in the project CLAUDE.md so every session in the repo applies it
options.D: Put the standard only in one lead developer's own memory for the rest to follow

questions.explanationCorrect: Codifying the standard in the project CLAUDE.md makes it load for every session in the repo, cheaply giving everyone one consistent style.
questions.explanationDistractor: Relying on each developer to remember the standard is exactly what produced the inconsistency in the first place.

questions.stem: Moving a proof-of-concept toward production, which set of additions most improves reliability and reviewability?

options.A: A flashier demo UI for the proof-of-concept along with some polished marketing copy
options.B: Removing the logging from the code to cut down on the noise in the program's output
options.C: Hard-coding all of the happy-path assumptions everywhere so as to keep the prototype's codebase simple for now
options.D: Retries with backoff, observability and logging, and eval gates around model and prompt changes

questions.explanationCorrect: Retries/backoff, observability, and eval gates are the reliability and reviewability additions that turn a proof-of-concept into something production-worthy.
questions.explanationDistractor: Removing logging reduces observability, making production incidents harder to diagnose rather than improving reliability.

questions.stem: You solved a recurring problem with a neat Claude workflow that other teams also face. What best turns your one-off into reusable organizational IP?

options.A: Contribute it as a documented, versioned skill or plugin to a shared repo or marketplace others can adopt
options.B: Keep the workflow local to yourself so that it stays your own competitive advantage
options.C: Describe the whole workflow just once out loud in a single team meeting and then simply move on from it entirely
options.D: Rewrite the whole thing from scratch each time another team comes and asks you for it

questions.explanationCorrect: Contributing a documented, versioned skill or plugin to a shared repo or marketplace turns a personal workflow into reusable, maintainable organizational IP.
questions.explanationDistractor: Keeping it local hoards the value and forces every other team to reinvent the same solution.

questions.stem: A shared content pipeline keeps drifting because people hand-edit the generated files. What structure prevents drift?

options.A: Let everyone on the team edit whichever of the files happens to be most convenient
options.B: Keep one canonical source, generate the rest via a build step, and never hand-edit generated files
options.C: Delete the build step altogether so that there is only ever one kind of file to manage
options.D: Store the generated outputs in a completely separate repo with no link at all back to the canonical source

questions.explanationCorrect: A single canonical source plus a build step, with generated files never hand-edited, keeps outputs in sync and prevents drift.
questions.explanationDistractor: Letting anyone edit any file is the cause of the drift, so it cannot be the fix.

questions.stem: Your accelerator behaves differently on each teammate's machine. Which practice most improves reproducibility for a shared tool?

options.A: Tell people to just update everything on their machine to the latest and then try again
options.B: Avoid documenting any of the versions or config at all, so that nothing whatsoever about the shared setup is ever pinned down or constrained
options.C: Pin and document versions and config (models, dependencies, skill and plugin versions) so everyone runs a known, reproducible setup
options.D: Rely on each person's local defaults for models and dependencies rather than pinning them

questions.explanationCorrect: Pinning and documenting versions and config gives everyone a known, reproducible setup, eliminating machine-to-machine variance.
questions.explanationDistractor: Relying on local defaults is precisely why behavior differs per machine, so it cannot improve reproducibility.

questions.stem: You are packaging a skill for wide internal use and want to guarantee it can never run destructive shell commands, regardless of who runs it. What is the durable way?

options.A: Add a comment near the top of the skill asking users politely not to misuse it
options.B: Trust the reviewers on the team to catch any misuse during the pull-request review
options.C: Document the destructive-command risk prominently in the skill's README for readers to notice
options.D: Constrain the skill with allowed-tools so the destructive capabilities are not available to it at all

questions.explanationCorrect: allowed-tools removes destructive capabilities from the skill entirely, a deterministic guardrail that holds no matter who runs it.
questions.explanationDistractor: A README warning relies on users reading and obeying it; it does not prevent the destructive command from running.

questions.stem: You want your Claude-generated changes to be easy for humans to review before merge. Which practice most supports that?

options.A: Produce small, focused changes with clear diffs and explanations, so reviewers can verify intent
options.B: Bundle several unrelated changes together into one large commit to save reviewer time
options.C: Skip writing any description entirely, on the theory that the code really ought to just speak for itself here
options.D: Force-push over the branch history so that only the final end state remains visible

questions.explanationCorrect: Small, focused changes with clear diffs and explanations let reviewers verify intent quickly, which is what makes generated work reviewable and defensible.
questions.explanationDistractor: Bundling unrelated changes into one large commit obscures intent and makes review harder, not easier.

questions.stem: A teammate wants to start using the plugin you published to your team's marketplace. What is the intended adoption path?

options.A: They must first clone your entire personal dotfiles repository to get the plugin working
options.B: They add the marketplace and install the plugin, getting its bundled skills and commands in a versioned, repeatable way
options.C: They copy and paste each individual skill file by hand out of a message in the team chat
options.D: They rebuild the whole plugin entirely from scratch on their own machine, using nothing but your short written description of what it does

questions.explanationCorrect: The intended path is to add the marketplace and install the plugin, which delivers its bundled skills and commands in a versioned, repeatable install.
questions.explanationDistractor: Manually copying each skill file is exactly the error-prone, unversioned process that publishing to a marketplace replaces.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, your shared CLAUDE.md and skills reference renamed services and removed endpoints, and Claude now makes stale-context mistakes. What is the durable fix?

options.A: Tell all of the users to simply and quietly skip over in their own heads whichever particular parts of the shared config happen to be wrong or outdated now
options.B: Add still more instructions on top of the file without removing the stale ones underneath
options.C: Treat shared config as living documentation and keep CLAUDE.md, skills, and .mcp.json current as the system evolves, since stale config is a leading failure cause
options.D: Delete all of the shared config and rely instead on the model's own training knowledge

questions.explanationCorrect: Shared config is living documentation; keeping CLAUDE.md, skills, and .mcp.json current as the system changes prevents the stale-context errors that are a top failure cause.
questions.explanationDistractor: Layering new instructions over the stale ones leaves the contradictions in place, so the model keeps making stale-context mistakes.

questions.stem: You are tempted to ship a heavyweight multi-command plugin for a task the team runs occasionally that a single well-described skill would cover. What is the best guidance for a maintainable accelerator?

options.A: Always build the single most feature-rich plugin that is currently available, purely in order to fully future-proof all of the work that lies ahead
options.B: Ship nothing reusable at all and just let everyone on the team keep solving it ad hoc
options.C: Put the whole thing in CLAUDE.md so that it loads for every single task across the repo
options.D: Prefer the simplest packaging that meets the need, a single skill here, and add plugin or marketplace machinery only when scope justifies it

questions.explanationCorrect: The simplest packaging that meets the need is the most maintainable; reach for a single skill first and add plugin/marketplace machinery only when the scope truly warrants it.
questions.explanationDistractor: Always building the most feature-rich plugin adds maintenance burden that an occasional task does not justify.
